newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese retailer Jusco raided over scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japanese retailer Jusco raided over scandal.

text.p: Tokyo prosecutors raided the headquarters of major supermarket chain Jusco Co Ltd on Wednesday, a day after its president was arrested for previous links to a racketeer payoff scandal involving Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd.

There was no suggestion that Jusco itself was involved in the scandal, but the string of actions by prosecutors tarnished the image of the nation's third biggest supermarket operator in terms of sales and hit its shares on the Tokyo bourse.
A Jusco spokesman told Reuters that three officials from the prosecutors' office had entered Jusco's headquarters in Makuhari, in Chiba prefecture near Tokyo.

"The prosecutors came to our Makuhari headquarters at 10.30 a.m. this morning and they are still here," the spokesman said, adding that he did not know the purpose of the raid. He could not immediately confirm whether or not Jusco's other offices and branches were being raided.

On Tuesday, four former DKB executives including Kenji Tanaka, now president of Jusco, were arrested and half of the 40 board members at one of Japan's leading commercial banks resigned in a shakeup which included the naming of a new president.

Tokyo prosecutors said on Tuesday that they arrested the former DKB executives, who were responsible for screening the bank's loans for irregularities, on suspicion of making illicit loans to a "sokaiya" racketeer. Sokaiya extort money by threatening to disrupt shareholders meetings.
Prosecutors said 39 separate loans, totalling 8.8 billion yen ($79.2 million), were believed to have been made through Daiwa Shinyo, a non-bank financial firm affiliated with DKB.
The affair has also ensnared Japan's biggest brokerage, Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

The scandal, which has now led to the arrests of 14 people, including four other DKB officials and a former Nomura president, is unfolding just as Japan kicks off its "Big Bang" reforms of its long-protected financial sector.

The Jusco spokesman said that it was not immediately clear whether Tanaka would step down. He said the company would hold a news conference later on Wednesday to be attended by its chairman Takuya Okada to comment on Tanaka's arrest.
On the Tokyo bourse, meanwhile, active sales hit Jusco shares, pushing them down 120 yen ($1) to 3,990 yen ($35.94) in early afternoon trade.
"The impact of the arrest on the share price is likely to be limited but the firm's image is going to be tarnished," a trader at a second-tier brokerage said.
Another trader said that the losses were not expanding as investors believed that the incident would not damage the supermarket operator's earnings.

Tanaka joined Jusco, a core firm of the Aeon group which comprises 150 firms across the globe, in May 1995 as an executive vice president from DKB, which is the main bank and the biggest shareholder of the supermarket chain. He took the presidency a year later.

In an interview last month, chairman Okada told Reuters that his company plans to more than double the number of its group firms that are listed on domestic bourses to about 30 by the year 2000. Jusco has alliances with such firms as Britain's Laura Ashley Holdings Plc and U.S. firms Talbots Inc, and Sports Authority Inc.
